title: Closed affine cones: dimension and irreducibility
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $N\in\mathbf N$. Write $P=\mathbf P(\{0,\ldots,N\};\operatorname{Spec}k)$ [def-nagata-projective-space-base-change] and $A=\mathbf A^{N+1}_k$ [def-sbc-affine-space], with coordinates $x_0,\ldots,x_N$ and origin $o=V(x_0,\ldots,x_N)$. For $i\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$ let $D_+(T_i)_k\subseteq P$ be the standard open and $u_{j/i}\in\Gamma(D_+(T_i)_k,\mathcal O_P)$ its coordinate functions as in [lem-weil-pbc-projective-space-standard-charts], so that $D_+(T_i)_k$ is affine with coordinate ring the polynomial ring $k[u_{j/i}:j\ne i]$, and let $D(x_i)\subseteq A$ be the open set where $x_i$ does not vanish, $D(x_i)=\operatorname{Spec}k[x_0,\ldots,x_N,x_i^{-1}]$. Then there is a unique morphism $\pi:A\setminus\{o\}\to P$ such that, for every $i$, $\pi^{-1}(D_+(T_i)_k)=D(x_i)$ and the restriction $D(x_i)\to D_+(T_i)_k$ is the spectrum of the $k$-algebra map $k[u_{j/i}:j\ne i]\to k[x_0,\ldots,x_N,x_i^{-1}]$, $u_{j/i}\mapsto x_j/x_i$. For each closed subset $Z\subseteq|P|$ define the subset $C(Z)=\{o\}\cup\pi^{-1}(Z)$ of $|A|$, where all subsets have their induced topologies. Then $C(Z)$ is closed. If $Z$ is nonempty and $\dim Z=d\in\mathbf Z_{\geq0}$, then $\dim C(Z)=d+1$, where dimension is topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. If in addition $Z$ is irreducible [def-weil-irreducible-components], then $C(Z)$ is irreducible. The convention for the empty set is $C(\varnothing)=\{o\}$.

source.place: Tag 0B2R, varieties-lemma-intersection-in-projective-space, proof, lines 6374-6404: the punctured affine-space projection, its standard charts and the closures of its inverse images.

proof.text: Put $U=A\setminus\{o\}$, $U_i=D(x_i)$ and $P_i=D_+(T_i)_k$. These opens cover $U$ and $P$. On $U_i$ the displayed ring map defines $q_i:U_i\to P_i$. On $U_i\cap U_j$ its image lies in $P_i\cap P_j$: the coordinate $u_{j/i}$ pulls back to the unit $x_j/x_i$. Indeed the standard-chart statement identifies $T_j=u_{j/i}T_i$, with $T_i$ a free generator, so $P_i\cap P_j$ is exactly the nonvanishing locus of $u_{j/i}$. On this overlap the pullbacks of the coordinates on $P_j$ are $(x_l/x_i)/(x_j/x_i)=x_l/x_j$, including $u_{i/j}=x_i/x_j$. Affine morphism extensionality therefore gives agreement with $q_j$. The morphism-gluing lemma gives $\pi:U\to P$ and its uniqueness. For a point in $U_j$, the same unit calculation gives $\pi(u)\in P_i$ if and only if $x_i(u)\ne0$. Thus $\pi^{-1}(P_i)=U_i$, proving all the required chart clauses.

source.place: Tag 0B2R, lemma-intersection-in-projective-space, proof: punctured projection and its displayed chart maps; omitted details supplied explicitly.

proof.text: Write $B_i=k[u_{j/i}:j\ne i]$. The local map is a Laurent-polynomial projection: $B_i[t,t^{-1}]\cong k[x_0,\ldots,x_N,x_i^{-1}]$ by $t\mapsto x_i$ and $u_{j/i}\mapsto x_j/x_i$. Its inverse sends $x_i$ to $t$, $x_j$ to $u_{j/i}t$ for $j\ne i$, and $x_i^{-1}$ to $t^{-1}$; both composites fix every algebra generator. The affine fibre-product formula, with the tensor-ring identification $B_i\otimes_k k[t,t^{-1}]\cong B_i[t,t^{-1}]$, therefore identifies $q_i$ with the first projection $P_i\times_k G\to P_i$, where $G=\operatorname{Spec}k[t,t^{-1}]=D(t)\subset\operatorname{Spec}k[t]$. In the tensor identification $b\otimes t^m\mapsto bt^m$ and $bt^m\mapsto b\otimes t^m$ are inverse maps.

source.place: Tag 0B2R, lemma-intersection-in-projective-space, proof: punctured projection and its displayed chart maps; omitted details supplied explicitly.

proof.text: Let $Z$ be nonempty, put $Y=\pi^{-1}(Z)\subset U$, and choose $z\in Z\cap P_i$. Set $L=\kappa(z)$ and $a_j=u_{j/i}(z)\in L$ for $j\ne i$. The ring map $k[x_0,\ldots,x_N]\to L[t]$, $x_i\mapsto t$, $x_j\mapsto a_jt$, gives $h:\operatorname{Spec}L[t]\to A$. At the generic point $(0)$, $t$ is nonzero, and the composite with $\pi$ has chart homomorphism $B_i\to L\hookrightarrow L(t)$ given by evaluation at $z$. Its kernel is the prime of $z$, so $h((0))\in Y$. At the prime $(t)$, every $x_j$ maps to zero and the contracted prime is $(x_0,\ldots,x_N)$, so $h((t))=o$. Since $(t)\in V(0)=\overline{\{(0)\}}$, continuity gives $o\in\overline Y$. This uses a residue field, not a rational point of $Z$.

source.place: Tag 0B2R, lemma-intersection-in-projective-space, proof: the origin is in the closure of every fibre; scalar-line argument.

proof.text: The subset $Y$ is closed in $U$, since $Z$ is closed and $\pi$ is continuous. Any point of $U\setminus Y$ has an open neighbourhood in $A$ contained in $U$ and disjoint from $Y$. Consequently $\overline Y\subset Y\cup\{o\}$; the reverse inclusion follows from the previous step. Thus $C(Z)=\overline Y$ is closed and $Y$ is a dense open subset of $C(Z)$. If $Z=\varnothing$, the definition instead gives $C(Z)=\{o\}=V(x_0,\ldots,x_N)$, which is closed. This proves the asserted empty-set convention without applying a nonempty-set dimension formula.

source.place: Tag 0B2R, lemma-intersection-in-projective-space, proof: punctured projection and its displayed chart maps; omitted details supplied explicitly.

proof.text: For the dimension calculation give $Z$ its reduced induced closed subscheme structure $Z_r\hookrightarrow P$. Its chart $Z_i=Z_r\cap P_i$ is $\operatorname{Spec}R_i$ for a quotient $R_i=B_i/K_i$ by a radical ideal. Form $Y_r=U\times_P Z_r$. Closed-immersion base change embeds $Y_r$ as a closed subscheme of $U$. On $U_i$ the affine fibre-product formula and step 2 give $\operatorname{Spec}(B_i[t,t^{-1}]\otimes_{B_i}R_i)=\operatorname{Spec}R_i[t,t^{-1}]\cong Z_i\times_kG$; the tensor isomorphism sends $b t^m\otimes r$ to $\bar b r t^m$. The primes in this quotient are exactly the primes of $U_i$ whose contractions to $B_i$ contain $K_i$, so its image is $\pi^{-1}(|Z_i|)$. Hence $|Y_r|=Y$, with the induced topology, and its opens $Y_i=\pi^{-1}(|Z_i|)$ have these product descriptions. Each nonempty $Z_i$ and $Y_i$ is finite type over $k$: its ring is generated by the finitely many coordinate images and, for $Y_i$, $t,t^{-1}$. The finitely many charts cover, giving finite type globally.

The ring $k[t]$ is a domain: the highest nonzero coefficient of a product of nonzero polynomials is the product of the highest nonzero coefficients. Its nilradical is therefore zero and prime, so its spectrum is irreducible. The ring dimension computation and the spectrum-dimension comparison give $\dim\operatorname{Spec}k[t]=1$. The open $G=D(t)$ is nonempty (it contains the zero prime), and the irreducible locally-algebraic open-dimension lemma gives $\dim G=1$. For every nonempty $Z_i$, the product-dimension lemma now gives $\dim Y_i=\dim Z_i+1$. Both factors are nonempty finite-type $k$-schemes, as required. The local-ring dimension comparison identifies the scheme dimensions used by that lemma with the topological dimensions here; isomorphisms of schemes induce homeomorphisms and hence preserve these dimensions.

source.place: Tag 0A21 (lemma-dimension-locally-algebraic), (3), and Tag 0B2M (lemma-dimension-product-locally-algebraic), (2); Algebra Tags 00ES, 00OQ and 00KE; Properties Tag 04MU.

proof.text: Suppose $\dim Z=d\geq0$. Open-subspace monotonicity bounds each $\dim Z_i$ by $d$. The open-cover bound gives the reverse inequality against the maximum of the dimensions of the nonempty $Z_i$. There are finitely many such opens and at least one; their dimensions are nonnegative integers bounded by $d$, so $d=\max_{Z_i\ne\varnothing}\dim Z_i$. Likewise the opens $Y_i$ cover $Y$, so monotonicity and the open-cover bound give $\dim Y=\max_{Y_i\ne\varnothing}\dim Y_i$. Each $Y_i$ is nonempty exactly when $Z_i$ is: a point of $Z_i$ lifts by $t=1$ over its residue field. Step 6 now yields $\dim Y=d+1$. The spaces to which the cover bound is applied are scheme spaces. The scheme-sobriety lemma gives a unique generic point for each irreducible closed subset, hence quasi-sobriety; it also gives $T_0$, since points with equal closures would be two generic points of the same irreducible closed subset. They have the required induced open-subspace topologies.

source.place: Tag 0055 (definition-Krull), open-subspace monotonicity, and Tag 0B7I (lemma-dimension-supremum-local-dimensions), chain argument.

proof.text: Give the closed subset $C(Z)\subset A$ its reduced induced closed subscheme structure $C_r$. It is affine, the spectrum of $k[x_0,\ldots,x_N]/J$ for a radical ideal $J$, and is finite type over $k$ since this quotient is generated by the coordinate images. Step 4 shows that $Y=C(Z)\setminus\{o\}$ is a dense open of $C_r$. The dense-open dimension comparison, which requires finite type but does not require irreducibility, gives $\dim C(Z)\leq\dim Y$. The reverse inequality is open-subspace monotonicity. Therefore $\dim C(Z)=\dim Y=d+1$, including $d=0$.

source.place: Tag 0A21 (lemma-dimension-locally-algebraic), componentwise dense-open consequence used in Tag 0BXV (lemma-dim-1-projective-completion); Schemes Tag 01J3.

proof.text: Finally suppose $Z$ is irreducible. Every nonempty $Z_i$ is irreducible: two nonempty relative opens in it are nonempty opens in $Z$ and hence meet. Its ring $R_i$ is reduced by the choice of $Z_r$, and its nilradical is prime by the spectrum irreducibility criterion; thus $R_i$ is a nonzero domain. The ring $R_i[t,t^{-1}]$ is also a domain: the highest nonzero Laurent coefficients of two nonzero finite sums multiply to a nonzero highest coefficient. Its spectrum $Y_i$ is therefore irreducible by the same criterion. For any two nonempty $Z_i,Z_j$, their intersection is nonempty by irreducibility of $Z$; a point there lifts to $Y$ by setting the scalar coordinate equal to $1$ over its residue field. Thus the irreducible opens $Y_i,Y_j$ meet. Fix one nonempty $Y_i$. In every nonempty $Y_j$, the intersection $Y_i\cap Y_j$ is a nonempty open and hence dense, so $Y_j\subset\overline{Y_i}$ and $Y=\overline{Y_i}$ in $Y$. A closure of an irreducible subset is irreducible: a decomposition into two closed subsets pulls back to such a decomposition on the dense subset. Thus $Y$ is irreducible, and the same observation applied to $C(Z)=\overline Y$ from step 4 shows that $C(Z)$ is irreducible.
